newsitem.title: SAUDI ARABIA: U.S. Defence Secretary carries tough Iran message to Gulf.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Defence Secretary carries tough Iran message to Gulf.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen met Saudi Arabian leaders on Saturday and said Washington was "hopeful but sceptical" that the recent election of a moderate cleric as Iran's president would end Tehran's support of international terrorism.

But Cohen also vowed in an interview with reporters who travelled with him to Jeddah that Washington would not soften its hard line policy toward Iran unless there were signs it had changed its attitude toward the West and its opposition to the Middle East peace process.

Cohen, beginning a visit to five Gulf states, was greeted by Saudi Defence Minister Prince Sultan and held talks with him and Saudi ambassador to the United States Prince Bandar. He was to meet later in the evening with King Fahd.
"We remain but hopeful but sceptical" on Iran, Cohen told reporters. "For the time being our policy is going to remain constant."

Referring to last month's election as Iranian president of Mohammad Khatami, seen as more moderate than his predecessor Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, Cohen said: "We need to see some signs on the part of the Iranians that this (election) will mark a change in their behaviour.

"As long as they continue to support terrorism, as long as they continue to develop weapons of mass destruction. as long as they try to upset the Middle East peace process, then our policy toward them is not going to change."
Cohen's visit will also take him to Kuwait, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates and Oman before flying home on Wednesday.

Some moderate Gulf states, including Qatar and Oman, have suggested that Washington should open a dialogue with Iran as a step toward ending U.S. attempts to isolate Tehran financially and diplomatically. Iran denies that it supports terrorism.

Cohen denied that there was any wavering in the policy of "dual containment" of Iran and Iraq on the part of the United States and the Gulf Cooperation Council of states in the region, adding that Saudi Arabia especially was a strong member of the team.

"We have strong support from all of the Gulf states for the dual containment," he told reporters, adding that the United States would welcome any good news obtained by those allies and any direct dialogue with Tehran.
"Obviously there are some people looking with hopefulness that this recent election represents a change," Cohen said.
"But we will have to wait and see. It will be some time before he (Khatami) settles into office and, I suspect, some time before physical changes would take place."

The Emir of Qatar, Hamad bin Khalifa al-Thani, met Cohen and President Bill Clinton in Washington earlier this week and told the Washington Post in an interview that he could not endorse the U.S. strategy of dual containment.
"With Iran, you have no more excuses," he was quoted by the Post as saying

It is Cohen's first visit as Secretary to the potentially volatile region where the United States sent more than 500,000 troops for the 1991 Gulf War in which a U.S.-led military coalition drove occupying Iraqi forces from Kuwait.

Washington still maintains a major naval fleet in the Gulf based in Bahrain and has nearly 200 attack jets in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait, keeping watch over southern Iraq. Cohen will visit some of the more than 4,000 U.S. airmen at Prince Sultan airbase in the Saudi desert on Sunday.

U.S. relations with the Saudis have at times been strained in the past year over Saudi handling of the investigation of a car bomb at the Khobar Towers military housing complex in Dhahran last June 25 that killed 19 U.S. airmen.

A similar attack at Riyadh in 1995 by internal Saudi dissenters woh oppose the U.S. military presence killed five American troops. But there was been no responsibility laid in last year's attack, including whether or not it might have been staged from outside the kingdom.

"So far, the evidence is still inconclusive and the investigation continues. We are not going to make any pre-judgment on that," Cohen said aboard his aircraft when asked if there was any evidence that Iran had supported the Khobar Towers attack.

"I don't have that perception, " he said when asked about continuing complaints from the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation that it had not been given full cooperation by Saudi Arabia including access to suspects in the investigation.
